items.title: Big Tech claims voters’ AI backlash is “anti-Trump” not “anti-tech”
items.summary: Tech industry in denial as US overwhelmingly votes to restrict AI, data centers.
items.content:
Donald Trump’s big, rapid American AI buildout now faces a major slowdown as voters in yesterday’s elections overwhelmingly supported candidates and measures that favored increasing restrictions on AI and data centers nationwide.

One resource from a polling firm, called Redbud Consulting, tracked data center initiatives on the ballot and reported that out of 44 measures across 10 states seeking to restrict data centers, 38 passed so far. Those measures included dozens of moratoriums and bans. Analysts suggested those won’t impact data centers already under construction or approved through 2027, instead largely impacting future projects planned for 2028. Only one measure passed allowing a data center to proceed. But even that small win represented pushback on the AI industry—requiring data center developers in a North Dakota city to pay for independent reviews and hold public hearings when expanding or proposing projects.

In addition to increasing regulations on data centers, voters also backed anti-AI candidates, electing officials vowing crackdowns in key states building out the most data center capacity in the US.

Most notably, Democratic challenger Gina Hinojosa won the Texas governor race that Axios reported would fundamentally scramble the math on Trump’s AI buildout. According to Bloomberg , Hinojosa’s election has developers facing down the “worst-case scenario.” Texas is the epicenter of the AI boom, Axios noted, and was expected to account for more than 41 percent of added data center capacity in 2028.

Now, Hinojosa plans to delay projects as long as it takes to pass laws “tackling impacts on water, electricity, air, and property rights.” Approximately “13 gigawatts of data center capacity” is now exposed, Bloomberg reported. Gordon Johnson of GLJ Research warned in a note that Texas projects with “power, permits and steel keep going,” but “those with power but no state environmental permits slip 12 to 18 months,” Bloomberg reported. Some projects may leave the state entirely, perhaps moving to Louisiana or Georgia—or perhaps going nowhere.

“She would impose a moratorium until legislation is passed that gives communities a voice, protects household utility bills, and ends the tax incentives for data centers,” Johnson’s note said. “The question now is how long the pause lasts.” As PIMCO head of public policy Libby Cantrill similarly warned, “even if statewide moratoria do not result, we expect to see a lot more sand in the gears of the AI buildout regardless—with more time required to secure permits and other approvals, as well as more concessions that data center developers will have to make.”

Texas wasn’t the only big shake-up. Democrats won governor races in the next three biggest states previously wooing data center developers—Arizona, Georgia, and Ohio. Overall, Axios projected that “nearly two-thirds of 2028 data center capacity” could face similar delays as Hinojosa threatens in Texas. Bloomberg estimated that half the data centers in the US are now more vulnerable to scrutiny.

For AI firms, that’s a nightmare, since any delays will set back revenue, and IT consulting firm Gartner recently estimated “the AI boom is nearly $5 trillion short of paying for itself.”

Likely soon, developers nationwide will face tighter rules limiting tax incentives and requiring stronger protections for residents around who pays for grid infrastructure and water use. Those kinds of regulations will most likely increase developers’ costs at an inconvenient time, Bloomberg’s report said.

While many reports suggested that the first so-called “AI election” proved the power of the people to rein in Big Tech, some AI industry insiders downplayed the election results on Wednesday. In a statement, Adam Kovacevich—a former Google executive and the CEO of a tech industry trade group and policy coalition called Chamber of Progress—suggested “the results offer little evidence of a voter mandate to crack down on AI or data centers.” He emphasized that “Democratic gubernatorial candidates who opposed data center bans won at a higher rate than those who supported them,” and admonished, “Let’s not confuse an anti-Trump wave with an anti-tech mandate.”

“Voters wanted change on the economy, not a crackdown on innovation,” Kovacevich said, while sharing a resource for those in the tech industry seeking an alternative spin on the results.

NBC News exit polls suggest it’s true that issues like cost of living or government corruption were ranked as more significant by voters than AI and data centers. However, like many analysts who point to AI opposition as a make-or-break issue for many voters, Alejandra Montoya-Boyer, vice president of The Leadership Conference’s Center for Civil Rights and Technology, disagreed with Kovacevich’s lens.

“The 2026 midterms have been the first true AI election in the US,” Montoya-Boyer said. “We saw voters turn up at the polls in record midterm numbers and vote for leaders who are willing to protect them and their rights from unchecked AI.”

Montoya-Boyer cited NBC’s polls showing that 3 in 4 voters are opposed to data centers. Additionally, more than half of voters said that “AI and data centers were a crucial or major factor in their vote for Congress.” The mass backlash is not just about utility costs or other data center fears, Montoya-Boyer suggested, but instead stemmed from a call from voters to regulate AI. Election day came “as the biggest AI companies raced to go public, AI systems broke out of the test ‘sandboxes’ meant to contain them, and biased and discriminatory AI kept making life-altering decisions about us,” Montoya-Boyer said.

“These results confirm numerous polls and what we civil rights leaders have been hearing from the communities we represent: Innovation is only real when it includes all of us and actually improves our lives,” Montoya-Boyer said.

items.title: Residential proxies detected on White House network
items.summary: https://krebsonsecurity.com/2026/11/want-to-rent-an-internet... Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50371246 Points: 1124 # Comments: 368
items.content:
Our Residential Proxy Observatory , launched earlier this week, is a first-of-its-kind interface that gives researchers a global view of residential proxy and anonymized internet activity.

While our team was looking through it, we noticed residential proxy exit activity on AS2650 . AS2650 is registered to the Executive Office of the President, the federal agency that hosts the White House network. Residential proxy services sell access to everyday devices, letting customers send traffic through them so it appears to come from that device's network.

From October 5 to November 3:

To make sure this was not a fluke, we checked these addresses against other residential proxy detection services, such as Spur and Synthient. Their public IP context pages independently identify these addresses as residential proxy exits.

This is public access. Anybody can obtain it by signing up to a public residential proxy service, paying a few dollars and sending requests through it. We did not selectively target this network or try to make our probes exit from it. We caught this by chance, simply by requesting global rotating access through these services.

Most of the activity happens in the evening, Eastern time: about half of it falls between 5 p.m. and midnight, and almost none happens in the early morning. That pattern suggests a person rather than a public guest Wi-Fi network: someone regularly on the White House network late into the evening, whose device is infected with a proxy SDK. Our data shows the exits, not the device or the person behind them.

Past research has shown that poorly secured proxy SDKs can allow internal network access and lateral movement. This is how past botnets have spread. In A Broken System Fueling Botnets , the researchers at Synthient documented how the Kimwolf botnet reached at least 2 million devices, mostly Android devices with an exposed ADB service, through residential proxy networks. If an SDK on this network has the same kind of flaw, anyone buying proxy access could use it to reach internal systems.

The White House is not the only surprise in the observatory. Residential proxies also reach some of the most isolated places on the planet.

Saint Helena, Ascension and Tristan da Cunha is the South Atlantic territory that includes the most remote inhabited island in the world. We recorded 413 addresses and more than 32,000 observations there, split between Starlink and the island's local internet provider, Sure Saint Helena.

We also recorded three observations from Antarctica . All of them come from a Cloudflare WARP address that points to McMurdo Station.

Other remote places with activity:

Residential proxies have infected every corner of the world, and it looks like there is no place they cannot reach. Layer3 Intel tracks residential proxy and anonymization infrastructure worldwide. Even when the proxies hide in networks on the farthest corners of the planet, we can still observe them, leaving threat actors no place to hide.

items.title: Insects don't swarm at LED lights
items.summary: Article URL: https://www.birdsoutsidemywindow.org/2026/11/03/insects-dont-swarm-at-led-lights/ Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50370610 Points: 279 # Comments: 134
items.content:
Remember when you used to encounter swarms of insects around outdoor electric lights? Their well known attraction to outdoor lights is used by entomologists and moth lovers to conduct insect surveys. All you need is a light and a white sheet to see who’s flying at night.

Nowadays, if you want to attract insects, you have to be picky about the light you use. As everyone changes over to LED lights, we see the color difference but we can’t see the crucial difference in insect attraction between incandescent and LED.

Our guide Roland Rumm on the WINGS Veracruz trip explained what happens with insects in the switch to LED lights. His family has an outdoor dining space that is well lit with artificial light. As a child he loved to watch the geckos climb to the lights and eat the insects. (This gecko can change to a bland gray color when he needs to.)

In recent years the family changed over to LED lights and the geckos disappeared. Were the geckos gone? No. But far fewer insects were attracted to the LED lights so the geckos had no reason to show up.

In 2024 the BBC wrote about Why insects are drawn to artificial light at night :

Flying insects use moonlight to navigate. Since the moon is always above them, they orient themselves so that the light shines on their backs. That’s how they stay upright in flight.

Moonlight contains ultraviolet (UV) and infrared wavelengths because it is merely reflected sunlight. Insects cue on UV, believing it to be the moon. When artificial lights transmit UV they look like moonlight so insects orient their backs to it. Consequently they circle the light and even flip upside down when the artificial light is pointing up to the sky!

Incandescent lights transmit UV but LEDs do not. Insects are far less attracted to LED.

In 2016 scientists at the University of Bristol, UK ran experiments to compare insect attraction to four types of light : Incandescent (tungsten filament), Compact fluorescent, “Cool-white” LED and “Warm-white” LED.

We conducted field experiments to compare the relative attractiveness of four commercially available “domestic” lights, one traditional (tungsten filament incandescent) and three modern (compact fluorescent, “cool white” LED and “warm white” LED), to aerial insects, particularly Diptera. We found that LEDs attracted significantly fewer insects than other light sources, but found no significant difference in attraction between the “cool” and “warm white” LEDs. Fewer flies were attracted to LEDs than alternate light sources, including fewer Culicoides midges (Diptera: Ceratopogonidae). Use of LEDs has the potential to mitigate disturbances to wildlife and occurrences of insect?borne diseases relative to competing lighting technologies.

Here’s what they found. NOTES: CFL = Compact fluorescent, FIL = incandescent (the old lightbulb), LEDC = LED cool white, LEDW = LED warm white light.

Typically LEDs do not emit UV light and are more energy efficient than traditional technologies. Electrical energy is converted almost entirely into electromagnetic (EM) radiation within the range of the visible light spectrum (400–700 nm) and therefore not wasted on producing wavelengths of light invisible to the human eye, that is, UV and infrared (IR). Thus, LEDs are less attractive to many insects than lights which emit UV light.

So that’s why there are very few bugs circling LED lights at night.

According to the BBC, this trait of LEDs is a good thing because incandescent (UV) artificial light at night distracts insects so much that they don’t reproduce, don’t feed, etc. Thus artificial light is considered a major reason why insect populations have declined. See: The impact of artificial light at night on nocturnal insects: A review and synthesis .

items.summary: Cruz and Trump seem to have no plans to fill FCC's empty Democratic seat.
items.content:
Senator Ted Cruz (R-Texas) is aiming to widen the Republican majority on the Federal Communications Commission before Democrats take over control of the Senate in January 2027.

Just before the Republicans’ midterm loss, Cruz yesterday announced a November 10 nomination hearing for Trump’s FCC nominee, Danielle Thumann Severs. In his final two months as chairman of the Senate Commerce Committee, Cruz seems set on moving the Thumann Severs nomination to a full vote of the Senate.

Confirming Thumann Severs would give Republicans an unusual 3-1 advantage on the FCC. That could become a 3-0 advantage at the end of 2027 because FCC Democrat Anna Gomez would have to leave the commission at that time if Trump does not agree to renominate her.

Senator Ron Wyden (D-Ore.) recently warned that federal law prohibits an all-Republican FCC and that “any action taken by a partisan FCC could be overturned in court, based on the statutory history of the Communications Act.” Wyden wrote in a September 24 letter to Gomez, “Because the Communications Act sets a quorum at three members, there is speculation that the President intends to fire you once [Thumann Severs] is confirmed, attempting to run the agency with an all-Republican 3-0 panel.”

“Under an all-Republican commission, every single license renewal, equipment certification, spectrum transfer, or other delegated action would be legally defective, casting a cloud of crippling legal uncertainty over the entire communications industry,” Wyden wrote.

Every FCC commissioner must be nominated by the president and confirmed by the Senate. By tradition, the president nominates opposing-party commissioners based on recommendations from the opposing party’s Senate leaders.

The bipartisan process has ensured that the FCC’s makeup complies with US law, but Trump hasn’t followed the tradition in his second term. He has failed to nominate a Democrat to the other empty FCC seat and has not renominated Gomez so she can continue past 2027.

Gomez today issued a statement calling on Congress to fill the empty FCC seats in a bipartisan manner.

“We must rebuild public trust in the FCC by returning the public interest standard to its original meaning as an obligation to communities rather than a tool for political pressure,” Gomez said. “That means defending the First Amendment and a free press from government interference, advancing competitive innovation that smartly protects our communications networks, and delivering real results for consumers.”

Thumann Severs is an attorney and senior counsel to FCC Chairman Brendan Carr. Trump nominated Thumann Severs in August , but a Senate nomination hearing originally scheduled in September was postponed to accommodate her maternity leave. We asked Cruz’s office about plans for Thumann Severs’ confirmation vote and will update this article if we get a response.

The Communications Act requires the FCC to have three members for a quorum. The US law also forbids supermajorities on the FCC by specifying that “the maximum number of commissioners who may be members of the same political party shall be a number equal to the least number of commissioners which constitutes a majority of the full membership of the Commission.”

In previous administrations, the president and Senate agreed on paired nominations to ensure that the president’s party maintained a 3-2 advantage. Senate Democrats have been pushing for the Thumann Severs nomination to be paired with a new Democratic nominee so the commission can have a full slate of five members. When it became clear that wouldn’t happen, Democrats asked Trump to at least renominate Gomez in order to maintain a 3-1 split.

Twenty-one Democratic lawmakers on the House Commerce Committee wrote a letter last week to Cruz and Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.), urging “that any new Republican nominee to the commission be paired with the nomination of a qualified Democratic commissioner, including the renomination of Commissioner Anna M. Gomez to a full term.”

The letter continued:

The Communications Act limits how many commissioners may belong to one political party, ensuring that decisions on broadband, media ownership, and network security are tested by more than one point of view… Robust disagreement, independent judgment, and deliberation strengthen the commission’s decision-making and provide an important check when the FCC considers policies with far-reaching implications for consumers, competition, and constitutional freedoms.

Gomez can’t prevent any major regulatory actions that Carr’s majority is set on taking, but she has been a consistent voice opposing Carr’s attacks on Trump’s least favorite news organizations and attempts to police speech on broadcast TV . She also has occasionally convinced Carr to make changes to rulemakings that she argued would harm telecom consumers.

The Democrats’ letter said Gomez has been a strong advocate for telecom consumer protections, competition, network security, and access to affordable high-speed broadband. “Additionally, the FCC’s licensing and enforcement authority over broadcasters carries real constitutional limits, and Commissioner Gomez has taken that seriously, defending editorial independence and speaking out when she believed that authority was being stretched beyond its proper role,” Democrats wrote.

Gomez’s term technically expired on June 30. US law allows her to serve until the end of 2027 or until the Senate confirms a replacement, whichever comes first. Severs would not replace Gomez because Trump nominated Thumann Severs to fill a different seat in a term expiring in 2029.

items.title: Ripple-65B Preview: U.S. Open-Weight SOTA on Agentic Coding
items.summary: Article URL: https://www.ricursive.com/ripple Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50369925 Points: 307 # Comments: 110
items.content:
Achieving U.S. Open-Weight SOTA on Agentic Coding

Ricursive Intelligence is a full-stack artificial intelligence lab building self-improving systems by co-optimizing hardware, software, and model.

To power our chip design platform, we trained a language model from scratch that sets a new U.S. open-weight SOTA on agentic coding. We optimized the model architecture for our training and serving platforms, driving substantial efficiency gains.

Today, we release Ripple-65B Preview , a general-purpose variant of the proprietary model that powers our AI chip design platform. The model is pretrained on 12 trillion tokens with support for up to 1M context length. Ripple-65B Preview delivers strong results on agentic coding, achieving U.S. open-weight state-of-the-art (80.52) on TerminalBench 2.1 and surpassing significantly larger US open-weight models such as Reflection Beam 501B (80.1), Meta Muse Spark Open 816B (76.4), Thinking Machines Inkling 975B (63.8), and NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Ultra 550B (56.4).

Ripple’s dense model architecture provides strong reasoning performance with low-latency token generation. The model’s small parameter envelope also enables it to run efficiently on local devices such as NVIDIA DGX Spark, which feature high compute FLOPs with low memory bandwidth relative to datacenter accelerators.

Ripple-65B Preview is available on Hugging Face , Together AI , GMI Cloud , and OpenRouter . Fireworks goes live later today.

LLM pretraining is legendarily expensive. In 2023, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said that GPT-4 training costs exceeded $100 million . In the following year, Dario Amodei said that frontier AI models can cost up to $1 billion to train, projecting that costs would rise to $10-100B by 2026 to 2027 for pretraining alone.

In contrast, we developed and trained Ripple-65B Preview for only $32M, which is one-tenth the cost of the previous open-weight SOTA on agentic coding , as estimated to the best of our knowledge. ¹ Note that $32M is our full R&D cost starting from scratch, including pretraining ladder development, data mixing, evals, debugging, synthetic data generation, posttraining recipe development, and the final hero pretraining and posttraining run.

Rather than investing in a brute-force RL climb, we carefully iterated on our SFT and RL recipes with a focus on compute efficiency. We opted not to buy any posttraining data, instead devising our own synthetic data pipelines, quality filtering, and coverage metrics.

Our mixed RL recipe uses truncated importance sampling , score centering , and linear length penalty with high-quality long-horizon synthetic environments. The RL tasks are tuned for our model capabilities, and we continuously added harder tasks as the model improved. The end result was a steep RL climb from a strong initial SFT checkpoint. We reached a TerminalBench 2.1 score of 80.5 with only 1.4M rollouts, roughly 70x fewer rollouts than Reflection Beam, the prior SOTA.

Ripple-65B Preview’s architecture was designed to be trained and served efficiently on NVIDIA hardware. A key objective was to make design decisions which reduce pretraining and posttraining infrastructure complexity while still enabling strong reasoning and agentic performance. Therefore, we chose to train a modernized dense Transformer model rather than use Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) like other labs. This decision quickly paid off, and we were able to train a strong model from scratch while maintaining a solid MFU (40%) throughout pretraining and posttraining, even with simple sharding, no custom kernels, and no quantization.

Ripple-65B Preview uses a thin-and-deep model aspect ratio, with a narrow d_model (5120) and 80 total layers. To improve reasoning performance, we overprovision the number of attention heads while increasing the SWA-to-global layer ratio and reducing SWA window size to compensate for the increased cost. In addition, we added FFN activation clipping , gated attention , global NoPE , and value residuals .

We optimized Ripple’s pretraining recipe through a series of careful model laddering experiments.

Our starting point was Olmo 3’s model ladder , from which we tested interventions at small scale with a focus on improving coding capabilities. Our v1.0 ladder implemented StepFun batch size and learning rate scaling laws, and v1.1 implemented our new ladder which smoothly scales architectural dimensions and model depth. Ladder v1.2 switched from the post-norm baseline to pre+post norm, which was neutral at small scale but showed improvements starting at 4B. Ladder v1.3 implemented sigmoid gated attention . Ladder v1.4 (2-stream mHC ) showed good results at smaller scale but did not improve at 4B scale, and was therefore rejected. Ladder v1.5 switched to global NoPE and added a final LR cooldown to zero, and ladder v1.6 added value residuals . In the final version, we switched to our custom pretraining dataset with substantially upsampled code.

Together, the compounded changes improved compute efficiency on code as measured by dolma_stack CE by up to 16x at 4B model scale. In other words, our final Ripple model ladder can be used to achieve similar code performance to the Olmo 3 ladder with 16x less compute . Note that the slope of the Olmo 3 ladder baseline is shallower than ladder v1.0+, which shows that the compute efficiency improvement will increase with additional scale.

We built Ripple-65B Preview to begin closing the loop between models and the hardware that fuels them. An internal variant of this model powers our AI chip design platform, and we look forward to seeing the capabilities that emerge as we scale toward the frontier.

We were fortunate to build on top of existing open-source contributions, including those from the Olmo team at the Allen Institute for AI (AI2), Prime Intellect, RadixArk, and NVIDIA. A strong open-source ecosystem is also self-improving, where contributors strengthen the ecosystem, which in turn draws more contributors.

items.title: Show HN: After a decade of reversing, I got co-op working in DOS Wing Commander
items.summary: Article URL: https://fireflyk64.github.io/wcmulti/ Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50369895 Points: 209 # Comments: 30
items.content:
Play it in your browser

When we were kids, my brother Patrick and I would steer our space fighter with one of us on controls and the other on the lasers and afterburner boost. We always dreamed of playing the Wing Commander series cooperatively as wingmates rather than as a two headed hydra in a single craft.

On October 4, 2015 as I was playing the classic Wing Commander in Dosbox I realized the whole memory probably fit in that 640K Bill Gates apocryphally said “ought to be enough for anybody”. If I could dump the memory and identify the locations that held the X,Y,Z coords for the player & wingman we could let the network packets control the wingman.

“I have to say that in 1981, making those decisions, I felt like I was providing enough freedom for 10 years. That is, a move from 64 K to 640 K felt like something that would last a great deal of time. Well, it didn't.” Source

This presented a clear problem to attack: out of fewer than a million bytes how would we identify that location? I decided to simplify the problem by trying to empty the game of other entities. A stopped player shouldn’t change coordinates. We could snapshot the memory twice when stopped to identify “background” memory churn. Then burst forward and measure again. If we didn’t turn (mouse was disabled) we might only change one axis. The next problem was to find an empty region of space. We had to start without our wingman Paladin, since he would move with us. After a miserable mission, letting the nefarious space cats overwhelm Paladin and running back to the spacecraft carrier, the Claw, the next mission was primed for a flight through empty space. I launched and flew directly ahead until everything despawned and took the memory snapshots using the DOSBox MEMDUMPBIN debug-command.

Now I had to discover anything that had not changed between the memory snapshots where my star fighter was in the original position but things that had changed when my star fighter moved.

(snapshot origin ⊙ snapshot later ) ∧ (snapshot origin ⊕ snapshot moved )

There were 35 distinct clusters of bytes that changed in the data segment. By inspecting these visually and looking for floats or small integer changes when I moved, I narrowed it down to a dozen locations it could be. I went to the chase camera view as well, and this helped to narrow it down to 13D3:A9C2 . I had the DOSBox debugger add integers at that address with its SM command and that caused the ship to jolt forward to a new location.

I had fun driving my ship around with the memory editor and reproduced it around the Claw and other NPC ships.

I set it down for nearly a year but in September 2016 I decided to write a small tool to automatically compare DOSBox snapshots instead of using the vbindiff GUI only. Directionality turned out to be more difficult so I set down the problem for a few more months and picked it back up in November.

To find the memory location of the rotation, I needed to look harder. As it happened the vectors were made of 4 byte scalars with 256 as 1.0 and valid positive vector positions between 0 and 255. This meant that most small rotations only changed a single byte. However, fortune was smiling on me that day because of what appeared to be a programmer joke at the time. Wing Commander reserved 64 slots for entity properties. In hex this would span numbers from 0x00 to 0x3F . However the programmers decided to use 0x3F for temporary usages and place the camera in 0x3D . Since 3D graphics were still nascent, the programmers may have thought it a good laugh to write 0x3D every time they needed to manipulate the 3D camera. That put a temporary variable two slots from the camera variable. And up and forward were also next to one another. This gave a nice wide region where I could locate those single byte changes. The first byte I understood was the y of the right vector; the print window I put around it happened to cover the camera's copy of up, which is where the overwrite experiment started. Furthermore, I rolled the ship over, and tripped sign extension, which caused all 3 adjacent bytes to switch from 0x00 to 0xff . Between these two facts, I noticed the temporary and camera bytes in the hex dumps. Writing to them did not help, since they were overwritten every frame, but luckily I wrote some extra bytes to the next vector as well, which was forward[0]. This caused a noticeable shift in the starfield and meant that I could now start investigating the code.

I put memory watchpoints on the addresses and traced the vector-add function called by the per-ship physics function called by a per-frame function and eventually the main loop.

It was now time to locate the byte sequences in IDA and start annotating the game. Wing Commander Multiplayer was now just a matter of repeating these techniques and figuring out how to puppeteer one ship from another's input.

December 2016 had shattered my illusion that we would be able to drive Wing Commander with writes to global memory alone. The details of manifesting laser fire or heat seekers were far too complicated to puppeteer solely from the addresses. We would need to co-opt the very functions in the original game to get the most accurate experience. One initial thought was to “will” the program counter to the right place, but we would need a way to insert arguments and return back from whence we came. Moreover, many of the functions were in various overlays that required indirection to invoke. It appears that Borland had a different overlay per compilation unit (C++ file) and they were dynamically loaded in different locations depending on the path the player took beforehand.

Patrick and I had to figure out a good trampoline system to call functions with the correct arguments. We chose the “Loading WING COMMANDER” string at 13D3:0187 and eventually 13D3:0395 “Sorry, an error has occured while %s”[sic] to hold the trampoline.

items.title: Texas was the new epicenter of the AI data center buildout. That might be kaput.
items.summary: Texas is the fastest-growing data center market in the US and ground zero for Big Tech’s largest AI buildouts. But the blue wave that swept the Lone Star State may jeopardize that position. Democrat James Talarico won the US Senate seat against Ken Paxton. Gina Hinojosa won the r
items.content:
Texas is the fastest-growing data center market in the US and ground zero for Big Tech's largest AI buildouts. But the blue wave that swept the Lone Star State may jeopardize that position.

Democrat James Talarico won the US Senate seat against Ken Paxton. Gina Hinojosa won the race for governor against the Republican incumbent, Greg Abbott. At the state level, Democrats will take control of the Texas House for the first time in 24 years. Talarico and Hinojosa made data centers a central issue, discussing them constantly on the campaign trail.

Even before the polls closed, insiders in the data center industry noticed that the times were changing. At the industry's DCD conference in Ashburn, Virginia, on Tuesday, panelists lamented that Texas had been the easiest place to build for years—until September. That's when Abbott, perhaps seeing the increasingly bipartisan distaste for these facilities , began changing course himself.

Developers said the governor’s office had stopped responding to their emails. On September 21, Abbott directed a key state regulator to halt data center permits. Many panelists at the conference were expecting this to mean that existing projects might be slowed and new ones could be halted altogether.

The governor-elect indeed seems eager to do that. Hinojosa supported tax breaks for data centers in 2023 as a way to boost construction jobs, but during her campaign she began pushing for a full-fledged moratorium.

That would be a problem for the hyperscalers of Big Tech, which have ambitious plans for AI training facilities in the state. The scale of projects already underway in Texas is massive. The Stargate Frontier data center in Shackelford County is projected to serve 1,820 megawatts—about as much as the nation’s largest data center, SpaceX’s Colossus 2 in Tennessee, and more than twice as much as the largest data center currently operating in Texas. Nexus Hubbard, also under construction and intended mostly to serve Anthropic, has a planned size of 6,400 megawatts and is the second-largest data center being built in the US, behind only Meta’s Hyperion project in Louisiana.

The potential for Democrats to order delays to these projects or moratoriums on new ones adds to growing anxiety that the AI buildout could stall. Banks and lenders are already getting pickier about the projects they back. And given the extent to which the data center buildout is underpinning growth in the economy right now, those forces combined could have ripple effects.

Voters around the country, though, were unambiguous in the midterms, sending a similar message on everything from state ballot questions to national offices. Voters supported efforts to protect ratepayers from increases in their electricity bills caused by data centers, and they favored some larger bans on new data centers altogether. If we needed any more convincing that Big Tech has fumbled its effort to sell voters on the idea that AI-powered abundance will make health care better, goods cheaper, and scientific breakthroughs more common, this was it.

A key question is whether the Texas counties with the largest data center presence were part of the reason these Democrats got elected, or if the anti-data-center vote came from elsewhere.

It’s complicated: The counties where much of the data center buildout is happening are around Dallas. Dallas County and others closest to it predictably went blue, but nearby Ellis County, which leads in permitting requests for data centers, went for Greg Abbott and Ken Paxton. Cameron County, near the state’s southern border, is a hot spot for data centers and voted blue in the midterms, which was a shift. But Mitchell County and Scurry County, where a bunch of projects in west Texas are located, went red.

This is a big deal, because no single office in the state decides whether a project goes ahead or is halted. Decisions often reflect an interplay between city governments, county officials, and state offices.

Local officials who have some say over data center development may resist sweeping restrictions from the state. And Democrats pushing for a moratorium might also face pushback from the construction unions that supported some of their campaigns. So while the blue wave spells a death knell for Texas data centers in theory, election winners may find that following through on their opposition once in office is much more complicated than campaigning on it.

items.title: A new Go API for JSON
items.summary: Article URL: https://go.dev/blog/jsonv2 Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50369106 Points: 336 # Comments: 170
items.content:
Michael Pratt, Joe Tsai, Daniel Martí, Johan Brandhorst-Satzkorn, Roger Peppe, Chris Hines, and Damien Neil 4 November 2026

JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) is a simple data interchange format, the most popular data format used on the internet, and widely read and written by Go programs. Go has included support for JSON in the standard library since well before Go 1.0. We first we wrote about support for JSON in Go more than 15 years ago!

Over time, packages evolve with the needs of their users, and encoding/json is no exception. Last year, we wrote about a new experimental API for JSON designed to bring long-awaited improvements and fixes.

After additional feedback and refinement, the new encoding/json/v2 and encoding/json/jsontext packages are stable and generally available in Go 1.27! This post is an updated version of the article introducing the experiment , describing the problems with encoding/json , and an introduction to the new packages.

Overall, encoding/json has held up well. The idea of marshaling and unmarshaling arbitrary Go types with some default representation in JSON, combined with the ability to customize the representation, has proven to be highly flexible. However, in the years since its introduction, various users have identified numerous shortcomings.

There are various behavioral flaws in encoding/json :

Imprecise handling of JSON syntax : Over the years, JSON has seen increased standardization in order for programs to properly communicate. Generally, decoders have become stricter at rejecting ambiguous inputs, to reduce the chance that two implementations will have different (successful) interpretations of a particular JSON value.

encoding/json currently accepts invalid UTF-8, whereas the latest Internet Standard (RFC 8259) requires valid UTF-8. The default behavior should report an error in the presence of invalid UTF-8, instead of introducing silent data corruption, which may cause problems downstream.

encoding/json currently accepts objects with duplicate member names. RFC 8259 does not specify how to handle duplicate names, so an implementation is free to choose an arbitrary value, merge the values, discard the values, or report an error. The presence of a duplicate name results in a JSON value without a universally agreed upon meaning. This could be exploited by attackers in security applications and has been exploited before (as in CVE-2017-12635 ). The default behavior should err on the side of safety and reject duplicate names.

Leaking nilness of slices and maps : JSON is often used to communicate with programs using JSON implementations that do not allow null to be unmarshaled into a data type expected to be a JSON array or object. Since encoding/json marshals a nil slice or map as a JSON null , this may lead to errors when unmarshaling by other implementations. A survey indicated that most Go users prefer that nil slices and maps are marshaled as an empty JSON array or object by default.

Case-insensitive unmarshaling : When unmarshaling, a JSON object member name is resolved to a Go struct field name using a case-insensitive match. This is a surprising default, a potential security vulnerability, and a performance limitation.

Inconsistent calling of methods : Due to an implementation detail, MarshalJSON methods declared on a pointer receiver are inconsistently called by encoding/json . While regarded as a bug, this cannot be fixed as too many applications depend on the current behavior.

The API of encoding/json can be tricky or restrictive:

It is difficult to correctly unmarshal from an io.Reader . Users often write json.NewDecoder(r).Decode(v) , which fails to reject trailing junk at the end of the input.

Options can be set on the Encoder and Decoder types, but cannot be used with the Marshal and Unmarshal functions. Similarly, types implementing the Marshaler and Unmarshaler interfaces cannot make use of the options and there is no way to plumb options down the call stack. For example, the Decoder.DisallowUnknownFields option loses its effect when calling a custom UnmarshalJSON method.

The Compact , Indent , and HTMLEscape functions write to a bytes.Buffer instead of something more flexible like a []byte or io.Writer . This limits the usability of those functions.

Setting aside internal implementation details, the public API commits it to certain performance limitations:

MarshalJSON : The MarshalJSON interface method forces the implementation to allocate the returned []byte . Also, the semantics require that encoding/json verify that the result is valid JSON and also to reformat it to match the specified indentation.

UnmarshalJSON : The UnmarshalJSON interface method requires that a complete JSON value be provided (without any trailing data). This forces encoding/json to parse the JSON value to be unmarshaled in its entirety to determine where it ends before it can call UnmarshalJSON . Afterwards, the UnmarshalJSON method itself must parse the provided JSON value again.

Lack of streaming : Even though the Encoder and Decoder types operate on an io.Writer or io.Reader , they buffer the entire JSON value in memory. The Decoder.Token method for reading individual tokens is allocation-heavy and there is no corresponding API for writing tokens.

Furthermore, if the implementation of a MarshalJSON or UnmarshalJSON method recursively calls the Marshal or Unmarshal function, then the performance becomes quadratic.

Introducing a new, incompatible major version of a package is a heavy consideration. If possible, we should try to fix the existing package.

While it is relatively easy to add new features, it is difficult to change existing features. Unfortunately, these problems are inherent consequences of the existing API, making them practically impossible to fix within the Go 1 compatibility promise .

items.title: Progress on provable inference for large language models
items.summary: Article URL: https://www.anthropic.com/research/provable-inference Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50368626 Points: 228 # Comments: 115
items.content:
Roy Rinberg (Anthropic), Alex Allain (Anthropic); Alessandro Chiesa (EPFL, StarkWare), Miranda Christ (MIT, RESI), Rahul Dalal (Anthropic STEM Fellows Program, Succinct), Giacomo Fenzi (EPFL), Ben Mayer (Anthropic Fellows Program, MIT), Guy Weissenberg (EPFL)

When you talk to a friend in person, you have many ways to know it is really them: you can see them, hear them, shake their hand. When you talk to an AI model, you have almost none. A user querying a model today cannot check that the responses came from the specific model that a developer claims is responding, as opposed to one secretly substituted in by a routing service for cost reasons, or even by an attacker who has tampered with the token stream. Judging from the model’s output alone is unreliable, even if it produces high-quality responses. Cryptographic proofs of inference solve this problem: they let a model provider commit to a model and then prove that each response was produced by that model. Such proofs could enable applications ranging from consumer products to internal security, and could contribute to a toolkit for verifying compliance with AI pacing requirements.

Specifically, we have made progress on a powerful type of cryptographic proof known as a “zkSNARK”, which is uniquely fit for provable inference (owing to its strong hiding and efficiency properties). In this post, we share some of that progress, primarily through a system we call FlashProve. A brief technical summary is as follows:

Today we are releasing five artifacts:

We release our code, Lean proofs, and documentation under the Apache 2.0 license. 1 This research post is meant to share intermediate progress, and not a completed research agenda. We are sharing this explicitly with the goal that others look at what we have done, take it, and improve it.

When a user sends a request to an AI model, today they have no way of knowing for certain that the model they selected is the one that generated the response. For everyday uses, in which users mostly care about the output and not necessarily which specific model produced it, this is a less pressing concern. But there are several cases where such assurance would be useful. For example, independent evaluators who test AI models before and after release need to know that the model they are evaluating is the model being served. Clients who use a model through a third-party routing service want assurance that the tokens came from the model they paid for. And if a cyberattacker modifies the token stream while pretending to be a given model, a user has no way to detect it from the output alone.

However, enabling verification of model responses is challenging. Most frontier models’ weights are kept private, and even if the user had access to the weights, checking that a given response was produced by a model with those weights would involve running the model, which requires computational resources far beyond what a typical user (or even evaluator) can afford.

The goal of provable inference (PI) is to enable a user with limited computational resources and without any information about the weights to verify that a response came from the requested model. PI is motivated both by a desire to increase customer trust in AI providers, and—because it can be used to provide assurances to independent evaluators and allows providers to demonstrate that they are meeting certain commitments and legal obligations—it also has implications for pacing the frontier of AI development and for AI regulation.

One way to implement PI is via a cryptographic object called a zero-knowledge succinct argument: the model provider sends, along with the claimed response, a short proof (say, a few megabytes) that the user can quickly verify (ideally, in seconds on a CPU). If the claimed response deviates from the specified model, the user’s check will fail. Importantly, cryptographic techniques ensure that the proof reveals nothing about the model’s weights.

Today, we release FlashProve: an open-source performant prototype for provable inference . For a 400B-parameter mixture-of-experts model (Llama 4 Maverick, 4-bit quantization), we show that a single H100 GPU generates proofs at over 100 tokens/second, with proof size of ~19 MB per 1,024-token request (~70-95 times the GPU time that vLLM, a common open-source library, takes to process prompts of the same length).

The release comes with executable code, Lean formalization, and a technical description of the protocol. Our aim is twofold: (i) accelerating and facilitating the development of provable inference; and (ii) demonstrating that zero-knowledge succinct arguments are practical for provable inference.

We believe that this progress has meaningful implications for security, in pacing AI development , in providing AI customers with integrity guarantees , in facilitating tooling for auditors and regulators , and more.

The development of artificial intelligence and its growing role in our digital infrastructure and economy raises trust challenges that AI providers must answer. Addressing these and other challenges is facilitated by relying on tools for provable inference (PI).

Tools for PI include hardware approaches, software approaches, or a combination of both. Here, we focus on a software-only approach: a cryptographic tool known as a “zkSNARK” ( zero-knowledge succinct argument of knowledge ). Informally, a zkSNARK is a system allowing a prover to convince a verifier , by way of a short “certificate”, that a given computation was executed correctly; crucially, the certificate is zero-knowledge in that it reveals no information beyond what is implied by the computation’s correctness and is succinct in that it’s exponentially faster to verify compared to the proved computation.

Below we outline several challenges and how zkSNARKs help in addressing them.

items.title: Kimi K3.1 Pro model weights are out
items.summary: Article URL: https://huggingface.co/moonshotai/Kimi-K3.1-Pro Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50366999 Points: 556 # Comments: 156
items.content:
📰 Tech Blog | 🚀 API Quickstart

Kimi K3.1 Pro is an open-weight, natively multimodal agentic model, and our most capable 3T-class model to date. Post-trained from Kimi K3 with large-scale joint reinforcement learning across hundreds of downstream domains, it is the first model in the K3.1 series. With a 1-million-token context window, Kimi K3.1 Pro delivers substantial improvements in coding, 3D creation, financial research, factual accuracy, and other agentic capabilities.

items.title: Guerrilla bike lanes: San Francisco makes illicit infrastructure permanent (2016)
items.summary: Article URL: https://99percentinvisible.org/article/guerrilla-bike-lanes-san-francisco-makes-illicit-infrastructure-permanent/ Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50366522 Points: 315 # Comments: 244
items.content:
When two cyclists were tragically killed in hit-and-run collisions this past summer, a group of anonymous urban activists known as the San Francisco Transformation Agency erected a set of protected bike lanes using traffic cones. Usually such guerrilla interventions are temporary. They raise awareness but ultimately get taken down by municipal authorities. But when the same group recently (and illegally) installed a set of soft-hit posts alongside Golden Gate Park, the city reacted by making the change official .

The SFMTrA , a play on the city’s Municipal Transportation Agency (SFMTA), “is a collective organization of men and women committed to making streets safer for cyclists and pedestrians, and doing it quickly.” According to the organization, their members use tactical urbanism to accomplish a range of objectives, including:

Many of their interventions involve orange traffic cones , which do grab visual attention but are also impermanent and easily damaged. Adding more robust traffic delineators (also known as soft or safe hit posts) may have helped persuade the city to retain this particular recent installation along John F. Kennedy Drive.

“Generally, we have no choice but to remove cones and posts that do not go through an official process,” wrote the city agency in a statement , “because it’s a code violation to place objects in the roadway, and they could create conflicts for various types of traffic.” But in this case, they plan to install official safe hit posts and leave the temporary ones in place until their review process is complete.

Guerrilla activists in other cities have tried similar things with mixed results. When the group Reasonably Polite Seattleites installed a similar set of delineators along a stretch of road in Seattle, the city initially took them down. Subsequently, though, officials wrote the activists an exceedingly nice response and eventually agreed to reinstall the posts.

City traffic engineer Dongho Chang of the Seattle Department of Transportation explained that a combination of issues (including the height of the posts and state control of the street) forced the removal at first. At the same time, he acknowledged the “time, money and risk” invested by the group and even offered to give the posts back. He later followed up with a letter indicating the city and Washington State Department of Transportation would put the delineators back in place.

In New York City, a perhaps less-polite group has been known to take things even further by building out entire bike lanes from scratch. After a local community board rejected plans to extend an extant lane, Right of Way took to the streets at night to paint their own. As a catalyst, the group cited an accident that took place after a taxi driver struck a pedestrian (after reportedly arguing with a cyclist sharing the lane).

Guerrilla interventions like these can provoke a variety of responses from critics and cities alike. In some cases, tactical urbanists are celebrated by communities but also jailed or fined by officials for their actions. In other instances, though, such installations can give a city an opportunity to publicly support a direction of change. In San Francisco, which has already built out 27 miles of protected bike lanes over recent years, the city seems to be signalling it is open to progress .

items.title: A Closer Look at Phonon TTS. Launching High-Quality On-Device Speech That Tops the Benchmarks.
items.content:
Two weeks ago, we opened up Phonon, our small text-to-speech model that runs on your own device. It needs no server and no network, and what you type stays with you.

We've been very happy with the reception so far. So here's the story of the launch: why we built Phonon, what it can do, the demos that came with it, and how it did on Hugging Face's Open TTS Leaderboard.

Most voice AI lives in the cloud: every sentence makes a round trip to a server. Phonon runs on your own device instead. Your text stays there and the voice works without a network. We’ve also opened the weights. Phonon 31m is Apache 2.0, so you can use it for free, even in a commercial product. The other models are CC BY-NC, so they’re free for non-commercial projects. If you’re building something commercial with those, pricing is based on your number of users, not how much speech you generate.

Getting a good voice to run on a small device has always been hard. You could make the model small, but then it didn’t sound great. Or you could make it sound great, but then it wouldn’t fit. We addressed both.

We announced Phonon in April and spent the next six months building on it with partners and early users. Their feedback helped us to shape this release. The models got smaller, and we added more languages and support for custom voices through voice cloning and voice design.

Phonon is based on the Pocket TTS lineage and as such uses flow matching to generate the audio which is very different from the modeling techniques used in other TTS systems. This is what allowed us to bring this level of quality to such a small model but it created new challenges while training the models. The training was initially numerically unstable and required several tricks to produce quality results on all five languages.

Phonon comes in two sizes, at about 65 MB and 75 MB. Together they speak English, French, German, Spanish and Portuguese. There are more than 100 built-in voices, and you can create your own in Gradium Studio . Phonon also handles the important things that most other TTS systems often stumble on, like phone numbers, dates and codes.

It runs on phones, laptops, single-board computers and in a browser tab, so you can hear it right now . Phonon 31m speaks English and is Apache 2.0, so you can build on it freely, including for commercial products. Phonon 40m covers all five languages under a non-commercial license.

The launch came with demos from friends and from our own team. On an Apple Watch with Wi-Fi off, Phonon talks you through a coffee brew step by step. On an iPhone with no signal, it counts your reps and keeps you going. A robot called Lamp, from Autonomous, wears a sorting hat and talks in character. In a browser, an offline dino runner becomes a radio show hosted by Rex. There's also a sci-fi game voiced on the player's own machine, and Proust read aloud page by page.

The Hugging Face team built the Transformers integration, so developers could use Phonon in Transformers from day one.

Developers have started building on it too. An ExecuTorch conversion runs Phonon on a visitor's GPU in the browser, Micdrop brings it to Node.js apps, and Spaces like smallest-s2s build on it.

Phonon was downloaded more than 200,000 times in its first two weeks, and it’s still trending on Hugging Face.

The Open TTS Leaderboard is a very new project from Hugging Face, and we love it. With more than 9,000 TTS models on the Hugging Face Hub , the leaderboard gives developers one place to compare open models and hear them side by side. Across 23 languages, models are evaluated on intelligibility ( word error rate of the outputs ), speed ( inverse real-time factor and time-to-first audio ), and naturalness ( UTMOS for English and KOMOS for Korean ). Fixed-voice and voice cloning are evaluated, with an additional speaker similarity metric for the latter. The leaderboard also has a Listen tab, where you can conveniently compare TTS outputs yourself and vote for the ones you like the most.

On intelligibility, Phonon ranks first in German and Spanish , and in the top three in every language we evaluated, next to models up to 100 times its size.

Speed is where we see Phonon truly shine, as the models top the CPU streaming benchmark on time-to-first audio.

We built a new inference framework, ptts , specifically for Phonon. The goal of ptts is to get the best performance on a wide variety of devices and as such supports more than 10 backends: CPU (Intel, Arm, WebAssembly), GPU (CUDA, Vulkan, Metal, WebGPU), and NPU (Apple Core ML, Snapdragon®).

Phonon is also available in 🤗 Transformers, from v5.21, as its reference PyTorch implementation. Where ptts runs a single stream on device, Transformers targets GPU throughput: batched generation, full-graph torch.compile , e.g., for synthesizing speech datasets at scale. Being native PyTorch, it is a base to build upon, whether to integrate Phonon into your own stack or to study the model itself.

It belongs to the Pocket TTS lineage, so we first added Pocket TTS to Transformers. Phonon sits on top as a modular model: about 200 lines describing only what differs.

Phonon generates audio latents autoregressively: each step outputs a latent that is fed back as the next input, and the training loss is computed on them. Latents are the model's inputs, outputs and targets, as text tokens are for a language model, so the codec mapping audio to latents plays the role of a tokenizer. Transformers ships it as such: an audio tokenizer , held by the processor next to the text tokenizer:

A voice is not a recording but a tensor of speaker latents. Phonon never encodes audio directly with its audio tokenizer, which ships decoder-only, and voices come precomputed: gradium/phonon-voices .
